conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days, and it helps us tell the difference between the “baby blues” that many moms experience and something that might need a little extra support. Everything you share stays between us, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through the questions one by one; each should only take a moment. Ready to begin?

To start, how have you been able to enjoy things lately—those little moments of pleasure or interest that used to feel good before the baby arrived?

[sighs softly, eyes on the blanket folded in my lap]

Honestly… most things feel kind of flat. I still smile when my little guy grips my finger or when my toddler brings me her drawing, but the spark is—muted, I guess. I made myself meet a friend for coffee last week; I kept thinking I “should” enjoy it, but I was just counting the minutes until I could go home and check on the baby again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, eyes still lowered]

Not really… I’ll chuckle if my husband makes a joke, but it feels forced. Mostly I’m too tired or worried to find anything genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet for a moment, then speaks softly]

Sometimes I’ll think about taking the baby for a walk in the sunshine, and that sounds a little nice—but when the moment comes, it feels like more effort than it’s worth. I used to get excited about little plans, like meeting a friend or even just a quiet bath, but now they hardly feel worth the trouble.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[wrings the edge of the blanket]

Yeah… I do that a lot. Last night the baby wouldn’t settle for two hours, and I kept thinking it must be because I drank that extra cup of coffee yesterday afternoon. If my toddler acts out at daycare, I’m sure it’s because I’m distracted and not giving her enough attention. Even silly things—like forgetting to buy diapers on the first trip to the store—turn into “I’m failing at this mom thing.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[exhales shakily]

Most days, yeah. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my chest feels tight—what if he stops breathing? What if I drop him? Sometimes I check the monitor every five minutes even when he’s napping fine. There’s no real reason, I just can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses fingertips together, voice a little shaky]

A few times this week it hit me out of nowhere—like yesterday in the grocery line, my heart just started racing and I felt I had to get out of there. I knew it didn’t make sense, but the panic still surged. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and watching every exit.
Things have been getting on top of me

[glances toward the baby monitor, then back]

Yes… even small chores feel huge. Yesterday I stood in front of a sink of bottles and just wanted to sit on the floor. I manage to push through, but it’s like I’m always one step behind, and the tiniest extra task makes me feel I could crumble.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[runs a hand through tangled hair]

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quiet. I replay every little thing I did with the baby—did I burp him long enough, did I skip tummy time? When I do drift off, I jerk awake sure I heard him cry—even if he’s still asleep. Some nights it takes over an hour to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be rocking the baby and tears just start rolling—no particular reason, just this heavy sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, voice cracking]

Yes… I cried twice yesterday. Once when I couldn’t get the baby to latch, and again after supper for no real reason. The tears just come and I can’t stop them, even when I know it’s “not a big deal.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[eyes drop to the floor, fingers tightening on the blanket]

A couple of times this week… nothing planned, just fleeting flashes—like when I’m rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and everything feels hopeless, I’ll think, “What if I just disappeared?” They’re quick, scary thoughts, not something I want to act on, but they pop in before I can push them away.

You've shared that the joy and spark you once felt has faded since the baby arrived: laughter feels forced, simple outings seem overwhelming, and chores like washing bottles feel insurmountable. Most days carry a gray cloud of sadness, tears come without warning, and nights are spent tossing with worries about the baby's safety. Fleeting thoughts of disappearing have surfaced during 3 a.m. feeds, and although you haven't acted on them, they frighten you. Your words paint a picture of a loving, committed mother who is doing her best while quietly carrying a heavy emotional load that deserves attention and support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only forced laughter in response to spouse, explicitly stating they "mostly... don't find anything genuinely funny," aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes diminished anticipation and follow-through for previously enjoyable activities, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive self-blame across multiple daily situations, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive worries multiple times daily with physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes unexpected panic episodes occurring multiple times this week with physical symptoms (racing heart, urge to escape), matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks like bottle-washing, and feeling on the verge of crumbling, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to intrusive worries and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness 'pretty much every day' with uncontrollable crying, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Crying twice in one day plus feeling unable to stop tears maps to "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 25 far exceeds the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses core symptoms nearly every day: persistent sadness, loss of interest, guilt, impaired sleep, overwhelm, and passive SI (score 2 on Q10). These map onto five <med>DSM-5</med> criterion A symptoms for more than two weeks, causing clinically significant distress and functional difficulty in infant care and self-care. High anxiety (Q4=3, Q5=2) is common in postpartum presentations. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for safety evaluation
2. Develop a written safety plan including 24/7 support person and crisis hotline numbers (988 or 1-833-943-5746)
3. Schedule initial therapy session within one week; evidence-based options include <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> tailored for postpartum mood
4. Begin gentle daily routine: 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced meals every 3-4 h, hydration, and brief rest when baby sleeps
5. Limit isolation: accept offered help from partner/friend for chores; plan one brief supportive visit or call daily
6. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track symptom change after treatment starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Client: Adult postpartum parent (≈ 2–4 wks post-birth per history)  
Source: self-report + non-verbal observations  

I. Presenting symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, crying spells (daily)  
- Marked guilt/self-blame re parenting competence  
- Difficulty initiating sleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings related to rumination  
- Overwhelming fatigue/“crumbling” under routine tasks  
- Free-floating anxiety, panic attacks (grocery line, nighttime)  
- Fleeting passive SI (“what if I just disappeared”) without plan or intent  

II. Pattern summary  
Symptoms cluster in depressive (mood, pleasure, energy, guilt) and anxious domains (worry, panic, somatic tension). Functional impact: basic infant care completed, but with perceived excessive effort; social activities avoided; partner provides primary auxiliary support.  

III. Screening significance  
EPDS equivalent items suggest moderate–high range for both depression and anxiety sub-scales; passive SI warrants immediate safety assessment.  

IV. Risk factors identified  
- Prior insomnia/heightened vigilance re infant safety  
- Lack of enjoyment in previously pleasant activities  
- Cognitive distortions (“I’m failing”)  
- Onset within first postpartum month  

V. Safety flag  
Passive suicidal ideation present; no disclosed plan, intent, or active thoughts of harm to infant. Recommend expedited psychiatric evaluation and safety-planning today.  

VI. Next screening step  
Complete EPDS (or equivalent) for formal score; facilitate warm-handoff to perinatal mental health or crisis clinician today; document capacity to maintain safety until follow-up.
